title: Beyond the Swing Justice
hook: The 'swing vote' is a lazy model of a nine-member court. Sort four terms of close cases and you get two distinct jobs: building narrow majorities, and bridging the dissents nobody won.
key_points: Feldman analyzes the 2022–23 through 2025–26 terms, the stretch when all nine current justices sat together.
'Majority makers' cross the ideological line to complete a narrow win; Roberts did so in 12 cross-bloc 5-4 majorities.
Roberts also appeared alongside the three liberal justices in 53 non-unanimous cases; Kavanaugh joined him in 7 of the pivotal majorities.
'Dissent bridges' join dissents led by the other bloc — Gorsuch did so in 8 of 46 dissents (17.4%), sharing nine with Justice Jackson.
'Coalition drift' tracks change over time: Barrett drifted most toward cross-bloc votes, while Thomas recorded no pivotal votes from 2023–26.
The upshot: Roberts anchors narrow majorities, Gorsuch anchors mixed dissents, and others act as smaller connectors.
content_html: Court-watchers love the idea of a single swing justice — one seat that decides everything. Writing at SCOTUSblog, Adam Feldman argues that the metaphor collapses once you actually sort the votes. Looking at the 2022–23 through 2025–26 terms, the span in which all nine current justices served together, he finds coalition-building split into distinct roles.
extra_html:
The first is the majority maker: a justice who crosses the ideological line to complete a narrow win. Chief Justice Roberts dominates that column, appearing in 12 cross-bloc 5-4 majorities and sitting with the three liberal justices in 53 non-unanimous cases overall; Justice Kavanaugh joined him in seven of those pivotal majorities, and Justice Barrett contributed one. The second role is the dissent bridge — joining a dissent led by the other bloc, which registers cross-bloc agreement in cases the group lost. Here Justice Gorsuch stands out, joining liberal-led dissents in 8 of 46 dissents (17.4%) and sharing nine dissents with Justice Jackson across a range of subjects; Barrett joined three, mostly environmental and administrative disputes.

Feldman's third measure, coalition drift, asks whether these habits change. Barrett showed the most movement toward cross-bloc voting, though on a small number of cases; Justice Thomas moved the other way, recording no pivotal votes from 2023 to 2026, and Justice Alito showed no change at all. His conclusion is a more textured map than "the swing justice decides": Roberts anchors the narrow majorities, Gorsuch anchors the mixed dissents, and Kavanaugh, Jackson and Barrett work as smaller connectors between blocs. The general lesson travels beyond this Court — on any multi-member body, the interesting structure is usually in who crosses lines and when, not in a single decisive seat.

related.title: Nine Justices, Nine Styles
related.hook: One scholar coded 5,095 questions from a full Supreme Court term and found each justice interrogates lawyers in a signature way — a fingerprint of how they think about the law.

related.title: Not All Dissents Are Created Equal
related.hook: Dissent tallies treat a one-line 'I would deny' the same as a fully reasoned opinion. One scholar sorted 386 of them on the emergency docket — and found about half were just bare votes.

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: The Power of a Dissent
related.hook: A dissenting judge loses the case — but a sharp dissent can outlive the majority, persuading future courts or pushing lawmakers to rewrite the rule.

flashcards.prompt: What is a 'dissent bridge', and why is it a separate role from being a swing vote?
flashcards.back_html: A justice who joins dissents led by the opposing bloc. It signals cross-bloc agreement in cases the coalition lost — invisible to any metric that only counts who supplied the winning fifth vote.

flashcards.prompt: In Feldman's data, which justice most clearly anchors the Court's narrow cross-bloc majorities?

Justice Jackson, who joined the most mixed dissents
